title: Same honest score, same false alarms?
hook: One risk score is equally honest for two groups. Who gets wrongly flagged?

knows: that a calibrated score means '80% means 80%' (say-seventy-mean-it)
doesNotKnow: that when two groups have different base rates, one calibrated score with one threshold must give them different false-alarm and miss rates, so 'fair' has to pick which equality it means

misconception: If a risk score is equally accurate (calibrated) for both groups and uses one threshold, it treats both groups' innocent people the same.
objective: The learner can explain that a score calibrated in two groups with different base rates flags a larger share of the higher-base-rate group's innocent people, and that the error rates match only when the base rates match.

claims.text: In the toy's kind of score, a high/low label whose reoffend rates among the flagged and among the rest are the same in both groups (honest in both), the two groups can have equal false-alarm and equal miss rates only if their base rates match, unless the label makes no mistakes (reveal: 'Otherwise no high/low score that makes mistakes is honest with matching errors.', after 'at 50, base rates match').
claims.source: v3 2026-10-16 (r6-ai A2): W-1379, cm-ai ruling (company/reviews/ai-cm-rulings.md 2026-10-16 r6): reveal uses the pre-approved fit fallback (the 17-word sentence cropped 16 px at 390x844); claim and reveal scoped to the toy's two-level label, support changed source -> derivation. Derivation (FC pass 35 and 62): with a = reoffend rate among the flagged, b among the rest, f = flagged share, p = af + b(1-f); FNR = b(1-f)/p and FPR = (1-a)f/(1-p); outside the perfect label (a = 1, b = 0) at least one is strictly monotone in f, so equal errors force equal f and so equal p. Note: Chouldechova 2017 and Kleinberg et al. 2017 state narrower or different conditions (equal PPV; balance of average scores) and are not the support. FC 62's counterexample shows the sentence is false for a calibrated score with more than two levels, which is why it is scoped; reset to unverified. | v2 2026-10-16 (r14 finding 3): 'Unless base rates match, no imperfect score is calibrated and equal on both errors' replaced by 'Otherwise no score that makes mistakes is calibrated with equal errors' (plain words for imperfect; the exception is a perfect score, a = 1 and b = 0 in FC pass 35's derivation); reset to unverified. | v1 record: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017), 'Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores', ITCS 2017 (arXiv 1609.05807); Chouldechova (2017), 'Fair prediction with disparate impact', Big Data 5(2): 153-163, eq. 2.1: FPR = p/(1-p) * (1-PPV)/PPV * (1-FNR); toy check A: 1 * 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2, B: 0.32/0.68 * 0.25 * 0.5 = 0.0588. About real systems; needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Rests on own derivation, not on Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan 2017 or Chouldechova 2017 (not opened, web blocked). With the lesson's sense of calibration (PPV = a and the low-group rate b equal across groups) and flagged share f: p = af + b(1-f), FNR = b(1-f)/p, FPR = (1-a)f/(1-p). FNR is strictly decreasing in f when a, b > 0 and FPR strictly increasing when a < 1, so equal errors force equal f, hence equal p, unless the score is perfect (a = 1 and b = 0). Chouldechova's identity FPR = p/(1-p)(1-PPV)/PPV(1-FNR) also follows from the definitions; toy check A 0.2, B 0.0588. | v2 FC note: FC pass 62 (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, SO-10-2 trigger d, shared server 3bf1d341, R3a pass; main checkout identical to server for this lesson): DISPUTED. True in the toy's sense and false as written. In the toy's sense (a high/low label whose two reoffend rates a, b are the same in both groups), my derivation from FC pass 35 holds: FNR = b(1-f)/p falls and FPR = (1-a)f/(1-p) rises with the flagged share f, so equal errors force equal f and equal p, unless a = 1 and b = 0. A grid check over a, b, f found 0 exceptions. But claim text and reveal say 'a score' / 'no score that makes mistakes is calibrated with equal errors', and that is false for a calibrated score with more than two levels and one cut-off. Counterexample (node, exact): levels 0.1, 0.3 (not flagged) and 0.6, 0.9 (flagged), each level's reoffend rate = its score in both groups. G1 100/100/100/100 people: base rate 47.5%, FPR 23.81%, FNR 21.05%. G2 0/320/90/340: base rate 60.8%, FPR 23.81%, FNR 21.05%. Both make mistakes (90 and 166). The published impossibility results are narrower: Chouldechova 2017 assumes equal PPV, and Kleinberg et al. 2017 assume balance (average scores), not thresholded error rates. Neither could be opened (arxiv.org, pnas.org, ncbi, ebi all 403). FIX (demo-builder, text owned by cm-ai): scope the sentence to the toy's kind of score, e.g. reveal 'Otherwise no high/low label that makes mistakes can be equally honest in both groups and have equal errors.', and the claim text the same way ('a high/low label with the same reoffend rate among flagged and among the rest in both groups'). Same fix for the recall 'why', which is an unrecorded learner-visible claim and is false for its own multi-level '30% risk' score: 'With different base rates a calibrated score cannot also equalise false alarms.' (G1/G2 above have equal false-alarm rates.) Record it as a claim and scope or reword it.
claims.note: FC pass mail-34bf (fact-checker, 2026-10-16, F-42 mailbox 20261016T154559740Z-evaluation-steward-49b534bf, main checkout bf6fde8 containing 169e88d; read Demo.tsx/model.ts and meta.json only, no builder notes; scratch scripts tails.mjs/port.mjs/cal.mjs recorded in the review file): VERIFIED (v3 wording, on its own terms). Learner text matches Demo.tsx: 'Otherwise no high/low score that makes mistakes is honest with matching errors.' after 'at 50, base rates match'. Own derivation: a = reoffend rate among flagged, b among the rest, both the same in both groups; flagged share f; p = af + b(1-f); FNR = b(1-f)/p with dFNR/df = -ab/p^2; FPR = (1-a)f/(1-p) with dFPR/df = (1-a)(1-b)/(1-p)^2. Both derivatives vanish only at (a,b) = (1,0) (perfect) or (0,1); otherwise at least one error is strictly monotone in f, so equal errors force equal f and so equal p. Node grid (a, b, f1, f2 in steps of 1/40, 2,687,960 pairs with different base rates): the only exceptions are a = 0, b = 1, the label that is wrong about everyone (FPR = FNR = 100%), i.e. the perfect label with high/low swapped; for any label where high means higher risk (a > b) there are none. The scope to a two-level label fixes FC 62's multi-level counterexample. Precision note for cm-ai, non-blocking: 'unless the label makes no mistakes (or is wrong about everyone)' would be exact in the claim text; the learner-facing 'high/low score' already implies a > b. Chouldechova 2017 and Kleinberg et al. 2017 are not the support (as the source says); not opened.

So a larger share of X's repayers is refused: with different base rates, this score cannot refuse both towns' repayers equally.'; answer 'A larger share of X's repayers are refused').
claims.source: New in v3 (r6-ai A2 item 3, W-1379: FC 62 found the v2 recall 'why' false for its own multi-level score). Derivation: with high share f, base rate p = 0.30f + 0.05(1-f) = 0.05 + 0.25f, so f = (p - 0.05)/0.25 rises with p; the refused share of repayers is 0.70f/(1-p), which rises with p (numerator up, denominator down). Builder's node 2026-10-16: p = 10% gives f = 0.2 and 15.56%; p = 20% gives f = 0.6 and 52.50%; p = 5% gives 0%; p = 30% gives f = 1 and 100% (everyone labelled high). 'Cannot refuse both towns' repayers equally' holds only when base rates differ, as the sentence says.

recall.question: A loan score labels people high or low risk, honest in two towns: in both, 30% of 'high' and 5% of 'low' people default. More of town X's people default. If 'high' means refused, what happens to people who would have repaid?
options: A larger share of X's repayers are refused
Both towns' repayers are refused at the same rate
A larger share of the other town's repayers are refused
recall.why: Each label is honest in both towns, so X, with more defaulters, has more people labelled high, and 7 in 10 of them repay. So a larger share of X's repayers is refused: with different base rates, this score cannot refuse both towns' repayers equally.
